questions.question: Compare the four market structures on the standard checklist — number of firms, nature of the product, entry, price control, demand curve shape and long-run profit — anchoring each structure to its example from the street: the fruit sellers, the water utility, the fuel stations and banks, and the spaza shops.
questions.expected_answer: Perfect competition — the fruit sellers outside the station: very many firms, identical products, free entry and exit, no price control (price takers), a horizontal individual demand curve at the market price, and only normal profit in the long run because new tables appear whenever margins fatten. Monopoly — the water utility: one firm, a unique product without close substitutes, entry blocked because nobody digs a second network of pipes, strong price-making power though still bound by demand, a downward-sloping demand curve with marginal revenue below it, and economic profit that can persist behind barriers, which is why a regulator watches its tariffs. Oligopoly — the fuel stations and banks: a few large interdependent firms, similar or differentiated products, high entry barriers, sticky prices explained by the kinked demand curve (elastic above the current price, inelastic below), rivalry through non-price competition, and lasting profits possible; collusion, overt in cartels or tacit through price leadership, is illegal. Monopolistic competition — the spaza shops: many firms, differentiated products (late hours, good bread, trust for regulars), easy entry, slight price-making power, a gently downward-sloping demand curve, short-run economic profit copied away by entrants until only normal profit survives.

questions.question: Explain the street's three blind spots — the taxi-washing bay, the community study centre and the streetlight — naming the formal market failure behind each, and match a corrective tool to each with its mechanism.
questions.expected_answer: The taxi-washing bay pouring soapy runoff into the stream is a negative externality: the wash price counts private costs only, so the harm downstream is priced at zero and the market delivers too much washing; formally, the supply curve based on private cost lies to the right of the social-cost curve, so output is too high and the price too low. Fix: a tax or charge on the runoff, which lifts private cost to social cost so the harm enters the polluter's own arithmetic. The community study centre is a positive externality: families weigh only their own benefit while safer evenings, better results and stronger future earners leak to every neighbour, so the street buys too little studying; formally, social benefit exceeds private demand. Fix: a subsidy that lowers the effective fee and raises use toward the efficient level. The streetlight is a public good — non-rivalrous and non-excludable — so free riding collapses private supply: nobody can be charged at the point of use, and no shop will build one for profit. Fix: direct provision by the municipality, financed through taxation. The pattern: price the harm, reward the spillover benefit, and provide directly what nobody can sell.

questions.question: Distinguish demand-pull from cost-push inflation using the street's telling of each, explain why the repo rate answers one better than the other, and state what the three-to-six percent target band is for.
questions.expected_answer: Demand-pull inflation is spending outrunning capacity: month-end crowds, bonus season and easy credit leave everyone flush, and shops mark up because they can — prices pulled from the till side. Its formal engines are credit booms, government expenditure and export surges. Cost-push inflation arrives from the supply side: the wholesaler's diesel jumps, the rand slips, the electricity bill lands, wages settle above productivity — and shops mark up to survive, prices shoved in through the back door. The repo rate answers demand-pull well because dearer credit cools consumption and investment, draining the excess spending that caused the problem; it answers cost-push poorly because no interest rate can cheapen diesel, end a drought or lower an administered tariff — it can only squeeze demand while the cost pressure remains, so the cure must match the cause. The three-to-six percent target band anchors expectations: households, businesses and lenders can plan rents, stock, wages and school fees a year ahead because they know where the central bank intends inflation to sit, and anchored expectations themselves slow the wage-price spiral. The honest evaluation: targeting has delivered credibility and predictability, but it remains a demand-side tool in an economy whose inflation often arrives from the cost side.
